FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey Resigns After One Year
One of FBI Director Kash Patel’s senior deputies is leaving the bureau, creating another opening near the top of the federal law enforcement agency. Andrew Bailey, a former Missouri attorney general who has served as one of the FBI’s co-deputy directors, announced that he will step down from his position.
Bailey said his final day with the bureau will be Friday, Oct. 2. “With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey said.
The announcement brings Bailey’s relatively brief tenure at the FBI to an end after he joined the agency in 2025. Before moving to Washington, Bailey served as Missouri’s attorney general and built a national profile through several prominent legal and political disputes.
He later became part of Director Kash Patel’s leadership team as the bureau underwent a broader restructuring. Bailey served in an unusual co-deputy director arrangement, placing him among the highest-ranking officials inside the FBI.
His departure comes during a period of continued personnel and organizational changes at the bureau. Since becoming FBI director in February 2025, Patel has pushed to reshape the agency’s priorities and leadership structure.
Patel has emphasized violent crime, counterterrorism, national security threats and internal accountability while arguing that the bureau should avoid politically motivated enforcement.
Bailey publicly supported those efforts and praised Patel as he announced his departure. “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence,” Bailey said.
Bailey also thanked President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for giving him the opportunity to serve in the administration.
During his time with the FBI, Bailey appeared alongside federal and state law enforcement officials during several operations and investigations.
He also helped promote the bureau’s increased focus on violent crime as Patel’s leadership team sought to change both the agency’s priorities and public image.
The FBI has faced sustained political scrutiny in recent years, particularly over allegations that certain investigations and enforcement decisions were influenced by partisan considerations.
Patel and his supporters have argued that changes are necessary to rebuild trust among Americans who have become skeptical of the institution, while critics have closely scrutinized the scope and consequences of the restructuring.
Bailey did not indicate that he had been removed or pressured to resign.
Instead, he said the decision was motivated by his desire to return to Missouri and spend additional time with his family.
Despite his departure, Bailey expressed confidence in the FBI’s direction and praised the work accomplished during his tenure.
His resignation now gives Patel another significant leadership position to fill as the bureau continues undergoing changes at its highest levels.

sources.news_title: Pulitzer reporter details 'lot of red flags' raised by FBI chief’s ouster
sources.text:
On Monday, the FBI deputy director who was leading up the 2020 election integrity probe resigned with just 35 days until the Nov. 3 election. It came just days after a report that tens of thousands of FBI agents and officials had their personal records stolen by hackers. So, the resignation of FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey "raises a lot of red flags," one veteran journalist reported. 
Speaking to MS NOW's Stephanie Ruhle, Carol Leonnig said that while President Donald Trump's administration claims it's taking the FBI hack "seriously," it's unclear whether it'll ever actually be capable of tracking down and prosecuting the hackers. 
"There's nothing they can do to kind of close the barn door, right? There's nothing that can be done," Leonnig said. "You can't hide that information after it's leaked out. It's kind of like your credit card or your Social Security number. Once it's out there, you're in trouble."
Bailey's resignation was yet another piece of bad news. It made Leonnig wonder if it's one of the reasons that Trump keeps banning MS NOW because they're revealing so much bad news about the president's administration. 
"The FBI is the premier law enforcement agency in the world, full stop, even though it's under a lot of challenge under the directorship of Kash Patel," continued Leonnig. "Now, this organization, which had two deputy directors installed."
She explained that this isn't normal. 
"These two people were installed because the White House was concerned that Kash Patel, as a director, had no experience in the FBI, which the president knew when he appointed him and nominated him and when the Senate confirmed him. But here he is in that job. So these co-deputy directors were installed once to help Dan Bongino. If anybody remembers the famous conservative podcaster," Leonnig added, explaining that Bongino, who has now left, lacked the necessary experience for the post, which is why extra people were needed. 
"I'm told by sources that [Bailey] was frustrated that an idea that was floated to him months ago, actually at the end of 2025, that he would eventually replace Kash Patel," Leonnig explained. "That wish never came true. And he was like, okay, you don't want me as a director. I'm out."
In public, Bailey has said that he was leaving to "spend more time with his family."
The reporter noted that it's an important thread to pull on, as Bailey was so involved in "overseeing election-related crimes and misconduct." There is a lot of pressure from the White House to prosecute election fraud for 2020, alleging that there was a widespread problem. 
Ruhle asked if that was a red flag to her, and Leonnig agreed. 
"It raises a lot of red flags. I'm not saying that I know with certainty," she said. "But I agree. It raises red flags. And as I say, it's a thread we should pull on about all of these people who are leaving, who had election-related sort of authority or portfolios, because it's happening across the Justice Department where people are saying, wait a minute, I don't want to do what the White House is directing the Department of Justice to do, when it might involve my professional reputation for life, my law license."
There's also a concern about future congressional investigations. Leonnig said that some of these people who resigned could end up as part of the Oversight Committee's questioning of those "who were ordered to do things by the white house that made them uncomfortable for lack of facts."

FBI deputy chief Bailey to resign after just over a year with agency
WASHINGTON — FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey said on Monday he is resigning his position, leaving the most prominent US law enforcement agency after a little more than a year.
Bailey, a Republican ally of President Donald Trump who left his job as Missouri attorney general to join the FBI, said he was leaving to return to his family. Bailey, serving under FBI Director Kash Patel, helped oversee election-related investigations and was present earlier this year when agents seized 2020 election ballots from Georgia.
ADVERTISING
“I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence,” Bailey wrote on social media.
The deputy director’s post, which oversees day-to-day law enforcement operations, has traditionally been apolitical and filled by career FBI officials. Trump has installed political allies in the role as he overhauls the agency to align with his agenda.
Bailey initially served as co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a former US Secret Service agent and conservative podcaster, who left the FBI in January.
Christopher Raia, a veteran FBI official, has more recently served as part of a three-person leadership team with Bailey and Patel.
Bailey joined the FBI following a series of high-profile stumbles by Patel, including botched handling of investigative files on late sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein that caused political headaches for the Trump administration and internal tension at the Justice Department.
The latest high-profile departure at the FBI occurred about five weeks before the US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has mobilized federal law enforcement agencies to investigate voting in elections by non-US citizens.
Bailey during his tenure at the FBI has helped manage the Trump administration’s investigations into election issues. The FBI has scrutinized election records from several states, but has not produced evidence to substantiate Trump’s false claims that widespread voter fraud led to his electoral defeat in 2020.

FBI Deputy Director Andrew Bailey Abruptly Resigns After One Year, Says He’s Returning to Missouri
FBI Deputy Director Andrew Bailey has abruptly resigned after one year on the job, according to The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and MSNOW. Bailey had been overseeing election matters. The reports did not explain why he resigned, leaving the reason for the sudden departure unclear.
Last August, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and FBI Director Kash Patel tapped then-Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey to serve as Co-Deputy Director of the FBI. The appointment moved Bailey from Missouri state government into a senior role at the bureau. He now says he is returning to his family in Missouri.
Later Monday morning, Bailey thanked President Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Patel for the opportunity to serve at the FBI. He credited President Trump’s leadership and described the administration’s work as historic. Bailey said:
“I want to thank President Trump, AG Todd Blanche, and FBI Director Kash Patel for the opportunity to serve in the FBI. Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again.”
Bailey added:
“With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri. I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.”
Bailey’s statement identifies his destination, but it does not provide a separate explanation for why he is leaving now. That is consistent with the reports, which said the reason for his resignation was unclear.
Patel responded by thanking Bailey for his service and crediting him with helping advance reforms at the bureau. Patel said:
“I want to thank Andrew Bailey for his dedicated service to return the FBI to its core mission and fulfill President Trump’s promise to make America safe again.”
Patel continued:
“Although Andrew is leaving the FBI in order to return to his family in Missouri, his fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on. Andrew’s leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve! Thanks Andrew for your tremendous dedication to the mission of this FBI.”
Bailey’s departure is also notable because of his record as a staunch Trump supporter. Before joining the FBI, he fought legal actions targeting President Trump and challenged prosecutors he believed were using the law against him.
In 2024, Bailey filed a lawsuit against the State of New York. He accused the state of launching an unconstitutional attack on the democratic process through its legal actions against President Trump.
His legal challenges also reached the U.S. Supreme Court. In 2023, Bailey filed a brief asking the court to halt Special Counsel Jack Smith’s move to circumvent the appellate court in Smith’s January 6 case against President Trump.
Bailey also took The Gateway Pundit’s First Amendment lawsuit against the Biden administration, formerly known as MO v Biden, to the U.S. Supreme Court. The Gateway Pundit’s founder and Editor-in-Chief Jim Hoft was one of the top five plaintiffs in that case.
For now, the public statements from Bailey and Patel focus on service, reform, and Bailey’s return to Missouri. Neither statement provides a fuller account of the circumstances behind the abrupt resignation.

sources.news_title: BREAKING: FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey RESIGNS — Cites Family, Praises Patel's Reform Mission
sources.text:
Andrew Bailey is stepping down as the FBI's co-deputy director, the bureau confirmed Monday, ending a roughly year-long tenure in a position that had never before existed at the agency. Bailey announced the move in a post on X, saying he is returning to his family in Missouri.
"With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri," Bailey wrote. "I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability and restore public trust in this institution of excellence."
Bailey thanked President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel for the opportunity, according to Fox News Digital. An internal FBI email cited family reasons for his departure, NBC News reported, citing two people familiar with the matter.
Patel praised Bailey in his own post on X. "Although Andrew is leaving the FBI in order to return to his family in Missouri, his fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on," Patel wrote. "Andrew's leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve!" In a separate post, the director added: "I want to thank Andrew Bailey for his dedicated service to return the FBI to its core mission and fulfill President Trump's promise to make America safe again."
Bailey, who served as Missouri attorney general before resigning that office to join the bureau in August 2025, was part of a leadership structure unprecedented in FBI history. He arrived alongside Dan Bongino, the former Secret Service agent turned conservative podcaster, in a two-person "co-deputy director" arrangement set up under Patel. Bongino departed in December 2025 after clashes with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi over the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, Fox News Digital reported. Bailey then served alongside Chris Raia, the former assistant director in charge of the bureau's New York City Field Office. Whether Raia now serves as the sole No. 2 — or whether the co-deputy structure persists — is not yet known, ABC News reported.
Bailey's fingerprints are on some of the bureau's most consequential work of the past year. ABC News reported that he helped lead election integrity investigations, including appearing alongside then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard at the January raid of the Fulton County, Georgia, election office, where ballots and other documents related to the 2020 election were seized. A federal judge in May denied Fulton County officials' request to force the FBI to return hundreds of boxes of ballots seized in that operation. As Missouri's attorney general, Bailey led an effort that ended in a consent decree barring social media companies from censoring protected speech, and filed numerous lawsuits against the Biden administration.
The resignation lands amid a broader churn in the bureau's upper ranks. NBC News reported that Patel is suing The Atlantic for $250 million over an article about his leadership, and has recently been in heated exchanges with Democratic members of Congress over his stewardship of the agency. Fox News Digital reported that two FBI agents were demoted and reassigned last week over concerns the bureau wasn't moving fast enough to investigate alleged threatening phone calls to Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. The FBI's Rapid Response account on X disputed claims that Bailey was "annoyed" over recent personnel moves at the bureau's Washington Field Office.
The White House deferred to Patel's remarks, and the FBI pointed Fox News Digital to Bailey's social media post.
Our Take
Read the statement Bailey actually wrote. He didn't cite burnout. He didn't cite frustration with the man he served. He cited his family — and then spent the rest of his post praising Kash Patel by name and predicting the reform work would continue. That is not the farewell of a man walking away from a fight. That's a man stepping off the field while the clock is still running his way.
Patriots, ask yourselves the question the legacy outlets won't touch: why is every single FBI exit by a Trump appointee immediately spun as chaos?" None of them led with the fact that Bailey's tenure coincided with the Fulton County raid that recovered 2020 election material, or the speech-censorship consent decree he won as Missouri's AG. The institutional press has one template for this administration — dysfunction — and it will not deviate for a man who went home to his kids.
Here's what actually matters. The co-deputy structure was always an experiment, an unorthodox answer to an orthodox problem: a bureau that had spent years treating half the country as a threat. Bailey and Bongino were the wrecking-ball phase. Raia, a career special agent out of New York, is the rebuild phase. That progression is not chaos — that is a renovation hitting its second stage.
What comes next is a test. Who fills the seat beside Raia? Does Patel consolidate the No. 2 role, or keep the two-man model that let him run reform and investigations in parallel? And does the election integrity work Bailey helped start keep its momentum through the fall?
Bailey answered the call once. The question now is who answers it next.

FBI Deputy Director Andrew Bailey resigns after one year in post
WASHINGTON >> Andrew Bailey, a deputy director of the FBI, said today that he would leave the job after a little more than a year, the second such departure amid the turbulence in federal law enforcement under the Trump administration.
Bailey said on social media that he was stepping down from his post, part of an unusual three-person leadership arrangement, “to return to my family in Missouri.” He expressed confidence that the FBI under the director, Kash Patel, would continue to fight violent crime, “ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.”
Patel in turn praised Bailey for making a “fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms” at the FBI.
In recent months, people familiar with the inner workings of the agency have described a rocky arrangement between Patel and his two deputy directors, Bailey and Christopher Raia, a longtime FBI agent and manager.
Patel and Bailey did not get along, and often went long stretches without speaking to each other, according to multiple people familiar with their interactions who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
It is unclear whether the White House will pick another second deputy director, or if Raia will become the only No. 2 in the bureau.

For decades, the bureau has had a single deputy director, a career FBI official who rose through the ranks of the organization and oversaw daily operations, while reporting to the director, who is appointed by the president. But President Donald Trump upended that tradition last year by naming right-wing podcaster Dan Bongino, who had little experience in law enforcement beyond serving as a Secret Service agent, as the No. 2 to Patel. In essence, that put two firebrand influencers with scant management experience atop the 35,000-person agency.
Patel and Bongino had a sometimes strained relationship with Trump’s first attorney general, Pam Bondi, whom they blamed for mishandling the release of files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. She in turn complained about Patel’s management of the bureau, including his propensity to post premature or inaccurate information about continuing operations.
In August 2025, the Trump administration announced a novel arrangement, saying that Bailey would join Bongino as a co-deputy director. At the time, Bailey was serving as the attorney general in Missouri, a post he had used to pursue lawsuits related to conservative culture-war issues.
Many agents inside the bureau believed that Bondi, a former Republican state attorney general, had brought in someone to serve as director in waiting if Trump ever tired of Patel. But Trump fired Bondi in April, and Patel outlasted Bailey.
In the interim, Bongino quit, and Patel selected Raia to replace him, keeping the three-person leadership arrangement rather than having Bailey become the sole No. 2. Patel more broadly appeared to sideline Bailey, who has left little imprint from his year at the bureau.
Bailey showed up in Atlanta in January, when the FBI executed a warrant to seize 2020 ballots from Fulton County, Georgia. His appearance was notable not just because of the effort to use the bureau to press Trump’s baseless claims of a rigged election, but also because it was extraordinarily rare for Bailey to play a visible role in any operation.

A leading anti-abortion zealot just quit the FBI
sources.text:
For the last year, the FBI’s co–No. 2 has been an anti-abortion hardliner oddly preoccupied with the earning potential of aborted fetuses. Back when Andrew Bailey was still the attorney general of Missouri, he tried to thwart a pro–abortion rights constitutional amendment on the 2024 ballot by arguing that “aborting unborn Missourians will have a deleterious impact on the [state’s] future tax base.” Later, in a lawsuit against the FDA over the abortion drug mifepristone, Bailey and other attorneys general claimed that telehealth access to abortion pills is “depressing expected birth rates for teenaged mothers,” potentially leading to a “diminishment of political representation” and “loss of federal funds.”
As arguments against abortion go, these were “absolutely insane,” one of Bailey’s Democratic rivals for AG declared. But pronatalist-tinged lunacy is hardly disqualifying in today’s GOP. In the summer of 2025, Bailey became co–deputy director of the FBI, a position that gave him enormous power over the agency’s operations—including, potentially, investigations against abortion advocates, providers, and patients.
But on Monday, in a sudden move that was no doubt deeply disappointing to his ultra-right allies, Bailey announced he is leaving the agency at the end of the week. He reportedly told colleagues in an email that he needed to spend more time with his family and followed up with a post on X.
MS Now reported that Bailey was upset about the demotions of two senior counterterrorism agents in the FBI’s Washington field office, who were supposedly removed from their jobs because FBI leadership was dissatisfied with their handling of a threat assessment involving harassing phone calls made to Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller. MS Now also said Bailey was frustrated at not being named to replace Kash Patel as FBI director, “a proposal once floated [after Patel] made numerous missteps and generated headlines that were unfavorable to the administration.”
Even in the wake of his departure, Bailey’s history of aggressive investigations into abortion providers in Missouri offers a chilling glimpse into what might happen at the federal level, as the Trump 2.0 administration faces growing pressure to ban or even criminalize medication abortion. Newly minted US Attorney General Todd Blanche has all but confirmed that a crackdown is coming, saying he would review the government’s stance on enforcing the Comstock Act, a 19th-century federal anti-vice law targeting “obscene” items sent by mail or any other means of shipping. Although it has long been dormant, Comstock was never repealed, and abortion opponents—including Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas—insist it remains the law of the land. Bailey’s suit against the FDA claimed that allowing telemedicine prescriptions of mifepristone violates Comstock, and he warned CVS and Walgreens that they’d run afoul of the statute by dispensing abortion meds.
At the FBI, Bailey was in a position to direct criminal investigations into the distribution of those medications—whether prescribed by clinicians across state lines or mailed by human rights groups to patients. In March, a group of Senate Republicans urged the FDA to work with federal law enforcement agencies to clamp down on mail-order services selling mifepristone. That’s exactly the kind of investigation the FBI would likely have overseen, said former federal public defender Peter Moyers, who represented a New York woman prosecuted by the DOJ during the first Trump administration for selling abortion pills.
Patel has expressed openness to criminal probes. During a September 15 hearing, Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley claimed that abortion-pill manufacturers are “actively coaching” people on how to use the mail and “other means of communication and commerce” to evade state abortion bans. “Without naming any of the companies—I’m not saying we’re not [investigating] already—but any use of the federal mail system is a federal crime that falls to the FBI to investigate, especially in conjunction with a violation of a state law that’s already on the books,” Patel said. “So we’re committed to that.”
Bailey didn’t have much of a public profile and had never run for office when, in 2022, he was appointed to replace newly elected Sen. Eric Schmitt as Missouri’s attorney general. The job has been a launching pad for many of the state’s best-known conservative politicians, from former Gov. John Ashcroft (President George W. Bush’s first attorney general) to MAGA showboat Hawley.
While Bailey lacked the Ivy League pedigree of many members of the state’s political elite, what he did share with other prominent Missouri conservatives—including President Donald Trump’s solicitor general, John Sauer; Trump White House counsel Will Scharf; and Ed Martin, the Stop the Stealer who helped write the GOP’s pro–fetal personhood platform in 2024—was an unwavering opposition to abortion. Bailey and his wife, Jessica, have four children, three of whom they adopted. In 2017, they lost a daughter who lived for only a few hours after birth. Bailey told the Missouri Independent that they’d received a fetal diagnosis “inconsistent with life” early in the pregnancy but chose to continue it anyway. “I have faith that God designs every human being in the womb,” he said then.
He also defended Missouri’s 2022 abortion ban that allowed the procedure only in the case of medical emergencies. “I want all kids to have an opportunity at life,” he said, arguing that the ban was “the proper policy position to protect life.”
Nonetheless, based on his work in the governor’s office, reproductive justice advocates had expected him to be “reasonable,” says Katy Erker-Lynch, executive director of the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization PROMO. That assessment ended up being “absolutely wrong.” Within months of taking office, Bailey was among the first red-state AGs to target providers of gender-affirming care, demanding that they turn over unredacted medical records of transgender minors—a move Trump’s Justice Department would emulate in 2025. He followed up by issuing an emergency rule that would have drastically limited access to such care for patients of all ages, withdrawing it only after the legislature passed its own ban on care for minors.
His focus on abortion bordered on obsessive. In 2024, he joined a lawsuit by religious doctors against the FDA over its regulation of mifepristone—a move that ended up keeping the litigation alive after the Supreme Court ruled the doctors didn’t have standing to sue. That same year, Bailey accused a Kansas City–area Planned Parenthood clinic of illegally “transporting” minors to help them obtain abortions, citing a staged sting video produced by the far-right activist group Project Veritas.
Meanwhile, he fought ferociously to keep Amendment 3, a voter initiative aimed at enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution, off the 2024 ballot, delaying the gathering of signatures and otherwise gumming up the process until even the GOP-dominated state Supreme Court ran out of patience. When he lost that campaign and voters went on to repeal Missouri’s abortion ban by a 52 to 48 percent margin, he litigated aggressively to keep restrictions in place, while accusing the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliates of providing medication abortions when they were not. Those efforts to subvert the amendment ultimately failed, despite a new state law that gave him special powers to intervene when courts blocked laws, and abortions have resumed. Now Missouri conservatives are trying to overturn the 2024 vote with their own ballot measure, also called Amendment 3, this November.
In one of his final anti-abortion initiatives as AG, Bailey sued the national office of Planned Parenthood for false advertising, arguing that it made misleading claims when it said that medication abortion is safer than Tylenol. Florida’s AG followed with a similar suit a few months later. Both cases remain active.
Records and internal correspondence obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight show that some of Bailey’s strategies may have come directly from anti-abortion organizations. For example, his claims that repealing Missouri’s abortion ban could lead to billions in lost tax revenue and federal funding echoed comments submitted to the state auditor’s office by Missouri Right to Life and the Heritage Foundation. Missouri Right to Life’s director also sent the Project Veritas sting video to Bailey’s office. Two years before Bailey filed the false advertising suit, his office received a memo from Students for Life of America outlining how state consumer protection laws could be used to attack access to medication abortion. Students for Life is now pushing the DOJ to revive the Comstock Act.
In response to questions about whether Bailey was present when Students for Life met with DOJ officials in May, the FBI said Bailey oversaw “a wide range of operational matters and interacts with a spectrum of stakeholders,” adding that he has “dedicated his career to upholding the constitution and enforcing the law.”
Bailey’s efforts on abortion didn’t distract from his fealty to the broader MAGA cause. He secured a “historic” $24 billion default judgment against the People’s Republic of China, among others, for misleading the public about supposedly starting the Covid pandemic, a legally pointless case he inherited from his predecessor, Schmitt. (China is now countersuing for $50 billion.) He tried to investigate the liberal nonprofit Media Matters for reporting on extremist content on Elon Musk’s X but was halted by a court. In a move that seemed calculated to prove his bona fides as a potential Trump attack dog, he sued the state of New York in the summer of 2024, arguing—unsuccessfully—that its prosecution of the once and future president for hush money payments to Stormy Daniels improperly interfered with Trump’s campaign.
After Trump’s victory, Bailey was reported to be on the short list to head the DOJ but, according to The New York Times, was deemed to be “too laid back” and “lackluster” for the president’s tastes. He lost out first to former Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz—who was forced to withdraw after sex trafficking and drug allegations proved unacceptable even to his former congressional colleagues—and then to ex–Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi. (Gaetz has denied the allegations against him.) Back in Missouri, Bailey doubled down on the kinds of cases sure to keep him on Trump’s radar, suing IBM over its diversity policies and Starbucks for allegedly discriminating against straight white men. IBM settled; Starbucks won a dismissal.
Eight months into Trump’s second term, Bailey finally got the nod to join the FBI as co–deputy director. It’s not clear why he was plucked for that role; what does seem clear is that far-right podcaster and ex–Secret Service agent Dan Bongino—who’d been doing the job solo for a few months—needed some adult supervision. (In response to questions for this story, the agency said Bailey’s “experience conducting complex investigations at the state level informs his management” in his FBI role.) After Bongino quit last winter, complaining about his long hours, career agent Christopher Raia became Bailey’s co-deputy.
In contrast with Patel, Bailey rarely made headlines in his FBI role. One notable exception was the agency’s raid in January on the Fulton County, Georgia, election office at the center of conspiracies around the 2020 election. Bailey, who has peddled election denialism, personally oversaw the raid, alongside then–Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard. Two Democratic senators called their presence during the search “unprecedented.”
The timing of Bailey’s resignation seems especially odd given his role in overseeing election-related matters at the FBI during the critical midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal noted that Bailey is stepping down amid massive staff turnover and other turmoil at the nation’s most important law enforcement agency.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again,” Bailey wrote on X. “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.” In his own post, Patel said Bailey’s “fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms” to the bureau “will live on.”
There’s nothing to suggest that Bailey’s departure will deter abortion foes from continuing to press the Trump administration from clamping down on abortion pills. Federal agencies have a host of laws to weaponize should they decide to come after providers, including Comstock or even the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, according to Rachel Rebouché, a law professor at the University of Texas at Austin.
Senate Republicans have called on federal agencies to work together to stop pills from coming into the country and being mailed between states, an effort the FBI typically would coordinate via a task force. Meanwhile, other diehard abortion opponents have been moving into influential positions in the administration, including pro–fetal personhood lawyer Josh Craddock at the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel and Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s new pick to lead the FDA. No one expects any big moves from the administration on the abortion front before the midterms. Then all bets are off.

After a little more than a year serving as the Federal Bureau of Investigation's co-deputy director, former Attorney General Andrew Bailey is stepping down and returning to Missouri, according to Bailey's social media.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again. "I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence."
In August 2025, Bailey announced his resignation from the attorney general position to serve as co-deputy director, first alongside Dan Bongino and then Christopher Raia. Catherine Hanaway was appointed by Gov. Mike Kehoe as Bailey's successor.
It's not currently clear whether another person will be appointed as co-deputy director or if Raia will serve as the FBI's sole deputy director.
According to reporting from the New York Times, people familiar with the inner workings of the agency said Bailey and Raia had "a rocky arrangement" with FBI Director Kash Patel, and that Patel and Bailey often went long stretches without speaking to each other.
However, following Bailey's X post, Patel responded on his own account:
"I want to thank Andrew Bailey for his dedicated service to return the FBI to its core mission and fulfill President Trump's promise to make America safe again. Although Andrew is leaving the FBI in order to return to his family in Missouri, his fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on," Patel wrote in the Sept. 28 post. "Andrew's leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve! Thanks Andrew for your tremendous dedication to the mission of this FBI."
In January, Bailey was present as FBI agents searched an election office in Fulton County, Georgia, for records related to the 2020 election.
Bailey is the second Missourian to step down from a federal position during the Trump administration. In August 2025, former U.S. Rep. Billy Long stepped down as IRS commissioner after less than two months to serve as ambassador to Iceland.

One of Kash Patel’s deputies resigns from the FBI
By Josh Campbell, CNN
(CNN) — Andrew Bailey, a senior FBI official and former Republican politician, told the agency’s workforce early Monday that he is resigning to spend more time with his family, two sources familiar told CNN.
Bailey served as Missouri’s attorney general before being hired by the FBI last year in an unusual move to serve as a newly created “co-deputy” to Director Kash Patel. He was brought on to split the FBI’s deputy director role with since-departed conservative podcaster Dan Bongino during a rift between Bongino and former Attorney General Pam Bondi over the handling of files pertaining to the investigation of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
It was widely speculated within the FBI that Bailey, whose focus at the bureau included election security issues, would eventually be asked to take the reins from Patel — a development that never materialized.
Bongino resigned earlier this year and returned to his podcasting career. He was replaced by a career senior FBI agent, although the “co-deputy director” model that included Bailey continued.
The position of FBI deputy director was historically filled by one career FBI agent who managed the day-to-day operations of the workforce of 38,000 people. It is unclear whether the agency will return to that precedent.
In a social media post Monday confirming his departure from the agency, Bailey touted the delivery under his tenure of “historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again” and said he would return to his family in Missouri.
As CNN previously reported, Bailey was originally under consideration to lead the FBI before Donald Trump’s second inauguration. He interviewed for the job with Trump in 2024 at Mar-a-Lago around the same time as Patel. Ultimately, Trump wasn’t impressed with the Missouri official, CNN reported, and said Bailey did not fit the mold of the legal bulldog the president-elect wanted to helm the FBI.
One source familiar with Bailey’s departure said relations between Patel and Bailey had quickly cooled shortly after his arrival at the agency last year and the two men were not close.
But in the announcement announcing his resignation, Bailey said he was “confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime” and to “defend the homeland.”
Patel responded to Bailey’s announcement on social media by thanking him for his service and for fulfilling the Trump administration’s mandates.

Bailey, a Republican ally of President Donald Trump, announced his resignation on Monday after joining the FBI from his position as Missouri attorney general. He served under FBI Director Kash Patel and was involved in investigations related to the 2020 US election.
Writing on X (formerly Twitter), Bailey thanked Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity to serve at the FBI.
“With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey wrote.

The FBI has examined election records in several states but has not produced evidence supporting Trump's claims that widespread voter fraud caused his defeat in the 2020 presidential election.
Bailey's departure comes about five weeks before the US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has also stepped up federal investigations into voting by non-US citizens ahead of the elections.
The FBI's deputy director position has traditionally been held by career bureau officials and was considered a non-political role. Under Trump, political allies have been appointed to senior positions as the administration seeks to reshape the agency.

He joined the FBI amid scrutiny of Patel's leadership, including the bureau's handling of investigative files involving late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which created political pressure for the Trump administration and tensions within the Justice Department.

FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey Steps Down, Citing Return to Family in Missouri
sources.text:
Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri attorney general who joined FBI leadership last year, announced Monday that he is leaving his post as co-deputy director, saying he intends to return to his family in Missouri.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
WASHINGTON — FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey announced Monday that he is stepping down after just over a year in the bureau’s senior leadership, ending an unusual tenure in which he shared the agency’s No. 2 position first with Dan Bongino and later with veteran FBI official Christopher Raia.
Bailey said publicly that his decision was driven by a desire to return to his wife and four children in Missouri.
“I want to thank President [Donald] Trump, @AGToddBlanche, and @FBIDirectorKash for the opportunity to serve in the FBI,” Bailey wrote in his announcement Monday. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again. With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri.”
“I am confident [FBI Director Kash] Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence,” the post continued.
Two people familiar with the personnel decision told Bloomberg Law that Bailey’s resignation will take effect Oct. 2. The sources spoke anonymously because they were discussing an internal personnel matter. Bloomberg reported that Bailey had informed colleagues Monday that he intended to leave Washington and return to Missouri.
FBI Director Kash Patel publicly thanked Bailey for his work and said the reforms he helped put in place would remain after his departure.
“I want to thank Andrew Bailey for his dedicated service to return the FBI to its core mission and fulfill President Trump’s promise to make America safe again,” Patel wrote in a Monday post. “Although Andrew is leaving the FBI in order to return to his family in Missouri, his fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on.”
“Andrew’s leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve! Thanks Andrew for your tremendous dedication to the mission of this FBI,” Patel added.
Bailey joined the bureau after serving as Missouri’s 44th attorney general.
He took office as attorney general in January 2023 after then-Gov. Mike Parson appointed him to replace Eric Schmitt, who had been elected to the U.S. Senate. Bailey remained in the position until Sept. 8, 2025, when he resigned to accept the federal appointment. His background and tenure in Missouri are summarized in his Ballotpedia profile.
At the time Bailey left Missouri, his office announced that he would become co-deputy director of the FBI. He had previously served as an Army officer with two deployments to Iraq, an assistant attorney general, assistant prosecutor and general counsel in both the Missouri Department of Corrections and governor’s office.
His appointment created an unconventional arrangement at FBI headquarters.
The deputy director has traditionally been the bureau’s single second-ranking official, responsible for overseeing day-to-day operations beneath the director. Under Patel, Bailey shared those duties.
When Bailey joined the FBI in 2025, he served alongside Bongino, a former Secret Service agent, conservative broadcaster and longtime Trump supporter who had become deputy director in March of that year.
Bongino remained in the position until early January 2026. Christopher Raia, a career FBI agent who had led the bureau’s New York field office and previously worked in counterterrorism, was subsequently selected to succeed him. Raia then became co-deputy director alongside Bailey. Reuters reported in January that the arrangement would leave both Bailey and Raia serving as deputy directors under Patel.
Bailey’s departure will leave Raia in the bureau’s senior operational leadership unless Patel announces another appointment.
Bailey publicly portrayed his resignation as an amicable departure, and Patel’s statement likewise praised his service.
Behind the scenes, however, some news organizations have reported tension between Bailey and Patel.
Multiple unidentified people familiar with the internal relationship told The New York Times that Bailey and Patel had not worked well together and sometimes went extended periods without speaking.
That account relies on anonymous sources and differs from the cordial public statements issued Monday by both men. Neither Bailey nor Patel cited disagreements between them as a reason for the resignation.
Bloomberg Law similarly characterized Bailey’s tenure as turbulent but reported that he told colleagues he was leaving to spend more time with his family.
Bailey’s exit is the second departure from the FBI’s deputy-director ranks during Patel’s tenure.
Bongino left in January after less than a year at the bureau. His appointment had been unusual because FBI deputy directors have generally risen through the agency’s career ranks. Raia’s selection represented a return to that model: he joined the FBI in 2003 and held a series of investigative and leadership assignments before taking command of the New York field office.
Bailey arrived from a different background.
As Missouri attorney general, he became a nationally prominent Republican legal official and participated in litigation involving the Biden administration, social media companies, abortion, transgender policies, federal regulations and legal proceedings involving Trump.
When Bailey announced his resignation as Missouri attorney general in August 2025, he described joining the FBI as another call to public service.
“It has been a humbling privilege to serve as the 44th Attorney General of the State of Missouri, and I am forever grateful to the people of Missouri for the opportunity to represent our state and your families,” Bailey said at the time. He added that “Missouri is and always will be home.”
He formally joined an FBI being reshaped under Patel, whom Trump selected to lead the bureau after returning to the White House.
The FBI’s own leadership page continues to identify Patel as director.
Bailey’s Monday statement credited Trump, Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche for giving him the opportunity to serve. Blanche became the 88th U.S. attorney general in August after previously serving as deputy and acting attorney general.
Bailey also said he believed the bureau had made substantial progress during his tenure, pointing broadly to violent-crime enforcement, homeland security, accountability and efforts to rebuild public confidence.
Patel echoed that assessment, crediting Bailey with helping institute reforms during the past year.
Neither man provided details Monday about who, if anyone, would replace Bailey or whether the FBI intends to continue operating with two deputy directors.

FBI deputy chief Andrew Bailey to resign after just over a year, cites family reasons
FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey is stepping down after just over a year at the agency, saying he wants to return to his family in Missouri. His departure comes amid a broader shake-up of the FBI under Director Kash Patel.
New Delhi: FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey has announced his resignation after just over a year at the US law enforcement agency, saying he is leaving to return to his family in Missouri.
Bailey, a former Missouri attorney general and political ally of US President Donald Trump, announced his decision on Monday. His last day will be Friday, according to an FBI spokesperson. “With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey said in a social media post.
He also expressed confidence in FBI Director Kash Patel, saying Patel would continue efforts to reform the agency, combat violent crime, defend the homeland and restore public trust.
Bailey oversaw election-related investigations
Bailey joined the FBI in August 2025 as one of two co-deputy directors, an unusual arrangement for an agency that had traditionally operated with a single deputy director. He initially served alongside Dan Bongino, a former Secret Service agent and conservative podcaster who later left the FBI. Christopher Raia, a veteran FBI official, subsequently became Bailey’s co-deputy.
During his tenure, Bailey was involved in election-related investigations. In January, he was present when FBI agents executed a search warrant at an election facility in Fulton County, Georgia, and seized ballots and other material linked to the 2020 presidential election. His departure comes only weeks before the November US midterm elections.
Latest exit in FBI leadership shake-up
Bailey’s resignation is the latest change at the FBI under Patel, who was appointed by Trump as director as the administration sought to reshape the agency.
The deputy director position traditionally goes to a career FBI official and involves overseeing the bureau’s day-to-day law enforcement operations. The decision to appoint Bailey and Bongino marked a significant departure from that practice because neither had previously worked as a career FBI official.
Bailey has publicly attributed his departure to family reasons. Other US media have reported tensions within the FBI leadership, including between Bailey and Patel, although those accounts have not been cited as Bailey’s stated reason for leaving.
Patel thanked Bailey for his service, crediting him with helping introduce what he described as critical reforms at the bureau.

sources.news_title: Andrew Bailey Announces his Return to Missouri
sources.text:
Andrew Bailey is stepping down as FBI co-deputy director, announcing Monday that he will leave the bureau and return to his family in Missouri.
Bailey, who served as Missouri’s attorney general from 2023 to 2025, joined the FBI last year after leaving the state’s top legal office to become co-deputy director under FBI Director Kash Patel. His resignation will take effect Oct. 2.
In announcing his departure, Bailey thanked President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity to serve.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again,” Bailey said.
Bailey said he was leaving with “great pride” in what the bureau had accomplished during his tenure and was returning to Missouri to be with his family.
During his year at the FBI, Bailey became one of the bureau’s more visible figures on violent crime, including through high-profile operations in his home state.
One of the most significant was Operation VIPER, a two-week federal initiative targeting violent crime across the St. Louis region that resulted in 91 arrests, 36 firearms seized and roughly $310,000 in cash recovered.
The April 20-May 1 operation brought together the FBI and law enforcement agencies in St. Louis, St. Louis County, St. Charles County and Jefferson County. Authorities said the effort focused on violent crime reduction, fugitive apprehension and removing armed offenders from the streets.
Authorities also seized approximately 600 grams of cocaine, one kilogram of methamphetamine and one kilogram of fentanyl, along with three vehicles. Six of those arrested were facing potential deportation proceedings.
“By getting the very worst of the worst offenders off the street in the spring, we hope to maintain the forward progress that we’ve enjoyed in the fight against violent crime,” Bailey said while announcing the operation’s results.
The FBI worked alongside local agencies, including the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department Fugitive Apprehension Strike Team, on arrests involving suspects accused of crimes including armed carjacking, first-degree assault and armed robbery.
The operation drew praise from Missouri officials, including Gov. Mike Kehoe and U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt, who highlighted the cooperation between federal, state and local law enforcement.
Bailey’s work at the FBI also took him beyond Missouri.
He recently traveled to Argentina and Guatemala, meeting with senior government, intelligence and law enforcement officials as the bureau worked to strengthen international cooperation and address terrorist and criminal networks before they could threaten the United States.
He also used his position to advocate for greater cooperation among law enforcement agencies. During an address to members of the FBI National Academy Associates in Canada, Bailey discussed attacks and threats against police officers and called for law enforcement agencies to stand together in responding to them.
Bailey brought that message back to Missouri during an address to the Missouri Fraternal Order of Police, where he discussed challenges facing officers, evolving threats against law enforcement and the importance of cooperation among federal, state and local agencies.
He also highlighted the FBI’s 2025 Reported Crimes in the Nation report, which provided a nationwide look at crime trends. The bureau said the data showed crime continuing to move in a positive direction and pointed to partnerships between federal, state and local agencies as an important part of those efforts.
Bailey’s path to the FBI’s senior leadership began with a rapid rise through Missouri politics.
Gov. Mike Parson appointed Bailey attorney general in 2022 after Eric Schmitt was elected to the U.S. Senate. Bailey had previously served as Parson’s general counsel and had never held elected office.
He went on to face a competitive Republican primary in 2024, defeating Trump attorney Will Scharf 63% to 37% to secure the GOP nomination.
Bailey then won the November general election, receiving 61.4%, compared with Democrat Elad Gross’ 38%.
The roughly 22-point victory was the largest margin among Missouri’s statewide candidates in the 2024 election, exceeding President Donald Trump’s margin in the state.
The win gave Bailey his first full elected term as attorney general after less than two years in office and further elevated his profile nationally.
He would later leave the attorney general’s office to take a leadership position at the FBI, becoming one of the highest-ranking Missourians in the Trump administration’s law enforcement apparatus.
Now, after roughly a year at the bureau, Bailey is returning to Missouri.
